copy.bottomLine: AI is showing up first in what firms buy and how people work: about 4 in 10 workers use it, and tech spending relative to payroll is the highest since the data begin in 1959. What's missing is a clear signal in jobs, pay or productivity. Output per hour and the AI-using industries are running ahead, but not yet beyond what chance often produces. Watch the December productivity revision and whether tech-services job losses deepen.
copy.changed: Latest releases: Q3 Productivity and Costs (BLS, Nov 5) put output per hour up at a 3.6% annual rate, so chance alone now explains the pickup about 10% of the time, down from 22%. Every test is now scored on the same three tiers; Work moves from Mixed to Not yet, because young graduates' edge was already small at the end of 2023 and has barely narrowed since.

caseFor.h: Workers and firms have moved fast.
caseFor.body: About 4 in 10 workers used generative AI for work in the latest surveys, averaging 43% over the last two readings against 36% a year earlier. Business spending on information-processing equipment and software has reached 10.7% of payroll, the highest since the data begin in 1959; the pre-2023 peak was 8.1%.

caseFor.h: Output per hour is pulling away.
caseFor.body: It has grown 2.5% a year since the end of 2023 on both main measures, against 1.6% and 1.4% in 2004–19, and at a 3.6% annual rate in Q3. Chance alone would produce a gap that large only about 10% of the time, down from 22% a quarter ago.

Professional and business services sped up 1.8 points more than retail, leisure and construction, each against its own 2010–19 pace; only 6% of 2010–19 stretches showed a gap that large. In information, where AI is built, output rose 8.2% a year while hours fell 1.5%.

Jobs in computer systems design are down 3.9% since December 2023, while all private jobs rose 1.5%. Only 11% of same-length stretches in 2002–19 were as bad, all of them right after the dot-com bust. Information jobs are down 7.6%.

Workers' share of business income is the lowest on record (the series begins in 1947) and has fallen 1.0% a year since the end of 2023, more than twice its 2004–19 pace. That fits firms substituting software and machines for people.

caseAgainst.body: Strip out more machines, more skills and harder work, and the SF Fed's figures show underlying efficiency growing about 0.1% a year since the end of 2023, below its 0.6% average in 2004–19. In the 1997–2003 boom it grew about 2.1% a year.

caseAgainst.h: Nothing is clear of noise yet.
caseAgainst.body: No counted test on this page is a clear signal. Chance alone would put output per hour this far above trend about 10% of the time, and labor's falling share about 35%. Eleven quarters in, output per hour is up 6.9%, against 9.1% at the same point in the 1990s.

caseAgainst.h: The job signs have older causes.
caseAgainst.body: Computer systems design jobs peaked in March 2023, as interest rates rose and before most firms used AI. Young graduates' edge over other 20–24-year-olds was already just 0.9 points at the end of 2023 and has narrowed only 0.2 since, a change matched in 63% of past stretches.

caseAgainst.h: Pay isn't moving the way the AI story predicts.
caseAgainst.body: If AI raised the value of people who direct work, management, business and financial pay should be pulling ahead of office support pay. Instead office pay has grown 4.1% a year since late 2023, against 3.8%, and the ratio is below its 2019 level.

caseAgainst.h: More machines and longer hours explain a lot.
caseAgainst.body: In the SF Fed's Q2 2026 figures, more capital and skills per hour added 1.7 points to 2.3% labor-productivity growth and working harder added another 1.7, while efficiency subtracted 1.1. Factory production workers average 42.0 hours a week, up from 40.8 two years earlier.

copy.headline: Use is spreading and spending is surging. Jobs and productivity show hints, but nothing yet clear of noise.

claims.claim: "Evidence is growing that we're turning the corner on productivity. US productivity grew at a 3.6% annual rate this past quarter. That's more than double the 1.5% average from 2007-2019."
claims.check: Q3 was 3.6% and the 2007–19 average 1.5%. But 17% of quarters in 2004–19 were as strong, and the 2.5% pace since the end of 2023 is suggestive, not clear: chance alone would produce it about 10% of the time. Underlying efficiency is flat.

claims.who: Alex Imas, Andrew Koh and Shane Legg, Google DeepMind (Oct 2026)
claims.claim: "Wages and job roles—not headline GDP or industry concentration—remain the earliest signals of change."
claims.check: Computer systems design jobs are down 3.9% since late 2023 against 1.5% growth in all private jobs, which is suggestive. But young graduates' edge has barely narrowed since 2023, and management, business and financial pay has slipped relative to office support pay (−0.6%), the opposite of the coordinator premium their model predicts.

claims.claim: "The SF Fed model is showing a slowdown in underlying productivity because it is attributing almost all of the pickup in output/hour to temporary cyclical forces associated with a hot economy."
claims.check: Underlying efficiency has grown about 0.1% a year since the end of 2023, below its 0.6% average in 2004–19, and working harder added 1.7 points to Q2 2026 growth. The industry data are a separate check: professional and business services sped up more than hands-on industries, a suggestive signal.
